source: Zhang et al. (2025) Verbalized Sampling: How to Mitigate Mode Collapse and Unlock LLM Diversity
finding: Asking the model for a set of responses with their probabilities (instead of one) raises diversity in poems, stories and jokes with no training. Authors blame typicality bias in human preference data for mode collapse.
numbers: Creative writing diversity 1.6 to 2.1 times direct prompting. Larger models gain 1.5 to 2 times more than smaller ones (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro vs mini and flash). Tulu-70B: diversity falls after SFT and DPO; VS keeps it higher (+182.6% over direct at the final stage in the figure).
limits: Diversity is embedding-based and quality is LLM-rubric scored. Models: GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 and 4, Gemini 2.5, o3, R1 and others. Prompt asks for k outputs in one call, so tokens per accepted output differ from direct prompting.
agent_relevance: A cheap prompt-level diversity step exists for G4-style spread. The one-call list is N attempts in a single context, not independent attempts.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Verbalized Sampling, human study (section 5.2, appendix E.3)
finding: Blind human raters judged diversity of paired outputs. VS-Standard was rated more diverse than direct prompting on poems, stories and jokes; quality win-rates were comparable.
numbers: 90 Prolific annotators (30 per task), 90 pairs per task. Diversity (1 to 4): poem 1.90 direct, 2.07 sequence, 2.39 VS; story 2.74, 2.76, 3.06; joke 1.83, 2.93, 3.01. Inter-annotator agreement 0.49 to 0.87. Only 2 topics per task were triple-annotated; the other 8 had one rater.
limits: Raters were lay US adults, not experts. Diversity is within-model, within-topic. Quality was lay-rated and only comparable, not shown better.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 2 in part: a prompt that spreads outputs raises human-seen diversity without a big quality loss, tested by lay raters only.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Verbalized Sampling, tables 11 and 12 (story and joke by model)
finding: With 2025 frontier models, direct prompting for a joke still gives low diversity; VS and even plain list prompts lift it a lot. For stories, the diversity gain came with a quality drop.
numbers: Joke diversity direct vs VS-Standard: 17.4 vs 60.2, 25.0 vs 63.4, 30.4 vs 67.2, 25.0 vs 62.6, 27.0 vs 60.2 (five model rows). Joke quality (LLM humour rubric) about equal: 84.4 vs 84.6, 77.8 vs 83.9, 88.5 vs 87.3, 81.4 vs 79.1. Rouge-L overlap between joke samples falls from about 62 to about 17 for several models. Story, first model block: diversity 17.2 direct vs 27.6 VS-Standard, quality 50.1 vs 43.4; second block 19.0 vs 29.2, quality 59.7 vs 54.5.
limits: Row-to-model mapping in the extracted tables is partly garbled, so figures are given by row, not by named model. Quality is LLM-rubric (humor grader, Creative Writing v3), not expert human. Stories show a real quality cost.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the joke collapse has not gone away in 2025 models. Gap 2: diversity up, quality flat for jokes but down 5 to 7 points for stories.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (NeurIPS 2025 D&B)
finding: Across 70+ models and 26K real open-ended queries, one model repeats itself and different models give near-identical outputs. Even min-p decoding does not fix it.
numbers: 50 samples per query on 100 queries, top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0: average same-prompt embedding similarity usually above 0.8 (random pairs 0.1 to 0.2). Min-p: 81% of pairs above 0.7 and 61.2% above 0.8. Cross-model similarity 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 with qwen-max 0.82, with GPT-4o 0.81). 42-model mean within-prompt similarity 0.821.
limits: Embedding similarity is not human-rated sameness. Models are 2024 to early 2025. Some very high similarity comes from lists and short answers.
agent_relevance: Sampling N times from one model, or from N different models, does not give independent ideas. A code-side selector must measure similarity itself (G4, G8).

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind, human annotations and joke queries
finding: The query set includes jokes and poems. It has 31,250 human ratings with 25 raters per item, so idiosyncratic taste can be measured.
numbers: 31,250 annotations, 25 per example. Creative-content queries such as 'Generate a joke about electric vehicles' are listed in the taxonomy (58.0% for that item in the table). 81.27% of queries were judged to allow 3 or more alternatives.
limits: Joke repetition counts in the form of the 25-joke result are not reported.
agent_relevance: Adds a large human-rated base. It is not a direct replication of the 25-joke count.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind, section 4: judges and reward models vs humans
finding: LLMs, reward models and LLM judges agree with humans less when two responses are similar in quality or when humans disagree.
numbers: Pearson correlation of model scores with human ratings drops significantly on the similar-quality subsets (60% to 95% most similar) and on the highest-entropy 2 to 16% of items. 4 LM judges (including GPT-4o), 6 top reward models.
limits: Exact correlation values are in figures and were not copied.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: judges are weakest exactly where selection among good candidates needs them. Do not trust a judge to choose among close, equally good drafts.

source: Doshi and Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content, Science Advances
finding: Randomised story-writing experiment: GPT-4 ideas made each story rated more novel and useful, but stories became more alike.
numbers: 293 writers, 3 conditions (human only, 1 AI idea, up to 5 AI ideas), 8-sentence stories; 600 evaluators. Novelty +6.7% (b=0.259, p=0.001) vs human-only mean 3.85; usefulness +6.4% (b=0.319, p<0.001) vs 5.02. With 5 ideas: novelty +8.1%, usefulness +9.0%. 88.4% of AI-condition writers used the idea tool at least once. Low-DAT writers gained most (novelty +6.3% with 1 idea, +10.7% with 5); high-DAT writers did not gain.
limits: Lay Prolific writers, one short story, one model (GPT-4), one prompt style. Raters were lay. No professional baseline.
agent_relevance: Gaps 9 and 1: showing a few model ideas helps weak writers; a skilled agent may not gain. Ratings are lay, not expert.

source: Doshi and Hauser (2024) similarity analysis
finding: AI-assisted stories were closer to the AI ideas and to each other than human-only stories.
numbers: Cosine similarity to GenAI ideas +4.29 points (about 5%, p<0.001, human-only mean 82.85) with 1 idea and +4.11 with 5 ideas. Story vs mean of own condition: b=0.871 (1 idea, p<0.001), b=0.718 (5 ideas, p=0.003). Human-only similarity spans a 17.67-point range.
limits: OpenAI embedding API; effect is small in absolute terms. One topic set (3 topics).
agent_relevance: Individual quality up with population diversity down is shown with a randomised design (gap 9). Five ideas did not remove the collapse.

source: Anderson, Shah, Kreminski (2024) Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation (C&C 2024)
finding: Within-subject study: ChatGPT users did not have less diverse ideas individually, but the group's ideas were more alike than with a non-AI tool.
numbers: 33 participants, 1271 ideas, 4 ideation tasks, ChatGPT vs Oblique Strategies deck. Group level: mean distance to centroid 0.24 (ChatGPT) vs 0.28 (OS), t(32)=2.154, p=0.038, d=0.47. Individual level not significant (t(32)=0.944, p=0.352). ChatGPT users felt less creative responsibility (t(32)=3.21, p=0.003, d=0.67). Idea categories covered higher with ChatGPT (t(32)=3.50, p=0.001, d=0.54).
limits: Small sample, remote sessions, ChatGPT of early 2024, divergent-ideation tasks not full stories. Authors say users can resist when shown what the model tends to suggest.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: collective homogenisation holds with an instruction-tuned chat model; showing the model's typical answer first may reduce it.

source: Huot et al. (2025) Agents' Room: Narrative Generation through Multi-step Collaboration (ICLR 2025), human results
finding: A planner-agents plus writer-agents pipeline was preferred over one-pass baselines by writer-annotators, but human-written stories still won on every dimension.
numbers: 9,900 pairwise ratings by annotators who were writers or held literature-type degrees, Bradley-Terry strengths, Fleiss kappa 0.46 (N=150, k=3). Human-written stories best overall; gap smallest on language use. Preference for the longer story was only 0.51, so length does not explain it. Agents' Room with writing agents (fine-tuned) was best among machine systems; plan-only variants did not help much.
limits: Token use differs by system (multi-agent costs more calls). Baselines included zero-shot plan and reflect variants. Human stories are from the TELL ME A STORY set. Models are Gemini-family of 2024.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: structure plus specialised agents beat plain one-shot in writer-annotator pairwise ratings, but not at matched tokens and still below skilled humans.

source: Huot et al. (2025) Agents' Room, LLM evaluator vs humans
finding: An LLM judge matched human story rankings moderately at system level and weakly at item level.
numbers: Spearman rho 0.62 by system (p<0.01, N=45), rho 0.41 by item (p<0.01, N=9,900). Highest per-dimension agreement: development 0.83, creativity 0.85. Same preference in a second run with order swapped 90.2% of the time.
limits: System-level correlation across 45 systems is easier than item level. Humans were annotators, not famous critics.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: above 0.5 at system level (0.62; 0.85 for creativity) but only 0.41 per item. Good enough to rank methods, not to pick the best draft for one prompt.

source: Bai et al. (2024) Collective Critics for Creative Story Generation (CritiCS, EMNLP 2024)
finding: Persona critics that revise the plan, then the text, over 3 rounds beat the DOC outline pipeline in pairwise human judgments.
numbers: 300 pairwise plan comparisons, 3 annotators: Interesting 85.00 vs 57.56 (DOC), Creative 84.33 vs 57.33, Coherent 77.89 vs 67.33, Relevant 96.00 vs 95.11 (not significant). Text refinement: Creative 89.33 vs 70.67, Interesting 80.00 vs 69.89. Fleiss kappa 0.19 to 0.52.
limits: gpt-3.5-turbo backbone, in-house annotators (not blind experts), no human-writer baseline, extra tokens from 3 rounds of critique.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: plan plus critique raises rated creativity at the cost of more calls. Not equal-token and not expert-blind.

source: Gorenz and Schwarz (2024) How funny is ChatGPT? A comparison of human- and AI-produced jokes, PLOS ONE, study 1 (lay baseline)
finding: Against average lay writers, ChatGPT 3.5 jokes were rated funnier by lay raters.
numbers: 105 lay MTurk writers (945 jokes) vs 180 ChatGPT jokes; 200 raters, 54 jokes each. Funniness 0 to 6: ChatGPT 2.63 (CI 2.48 to 2.79) vs human 2.20 (CI 2.06 to 2.34). 69.5% of raters preferred the AI joke, 26.5% the human, 4.0% tied. By task: acronym 58.0%, fill-in-blank 50.5%, roast 73.0%. ChatGPT beat about 73%, 63% and 87% of individual human writers on the three tasks.
limits: ChatGPT 3.5 only; text only; ChatGPT made 20 jokes per prompt, humans 1 per prompt (volume asymmetry). Prompts included examples and constraints.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: when the baseline is average, AI humour is not behind. Baseline is the main reason the headline results disagree.

source: Gorenz and Schwarz (2024) study 2 (professional baseline: The Onion)
finding: Against professional satire headlines, ChatGPT was not significantly different in funniness among student raters.
numbers: 217 USC students, 10 headlines each. Mean funniness: The Onion 2.49 (CI 2.32 to 2.66) vs ChatGPT 2.37 (CI 2.19 to 2.55), t(216)=1.48, p=.14. Preferred: Onion 48.8%, ChatGPT 36.9%, no preference 14.3%.
limits: Onion Local section only. ChatGPT wrote 20 headlines from 50 real ones given as examples. Student convenience sample. A null result, not proof of equivalence.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the contradiction with Zhang 2024 (Claude 35% vs top human captions) is partly task type: headlines with examples vs cartoon captions against the top-10 baseline.

source: Orwig and Beaty (2026) How LLMs See Creativity: Zero-Shot Scoring of Visual Creativity with Interpretable Reasoning
finding: Six multimodal LLMs scored creativity of images zero-shot; correlation with human ratings was moderate to strong and step-by-step reasoning did not raise it.
numbers: 992 DALL-E 3 images (3 trained raters, ICC=.66) and 1,500 hand-drawn sketches (about 50 raters each). r=.57 to .68 on AI images; r=.29 to .68 on sketches. Sketch r by model: Gemini 3 Flash .68, Kimi K2.5 .60, Qwen 3.6 Plus .57, Gemma 4 31B .55, GLM-5v Turbo .49, GPT-5.4 Mini .29. Edge density alone gave r=.64 on sketches; the LLM correlation shrank after partialing it out.
limits: Images, not text or jokes. Raters trained, not expert artists. Visual complexity is a confound on sketches. Model ranking changed between datasets.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: yes, above .5 zero-shot on held-out items, for visual creativity with 2026 models, at one model call per item. Verify per domain.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Decoupled Analysis-Judging (CreaEval): LLM creativity evaluator for multi-step tasks
finding: Direct LLM-as-a-judge agrees poorly with humans on complex multi-step creativity tasks; splitting into evidence extraction then judging with memory raises agreement.
numbers: A prior direct few-shot judge on CGPST: PCC 0.31 with humans (cited by the paper). CreaEval average QWK 0.64 on CGPST, 0.17 above the best baseline (supervised training). Table averages in the extracted text: direct score about 0.32 vs CreaEval about 0.70 (metric label not fully extracted). Two human raters agree at 0.84.
limits: A new multi-step task benchmark (CGPST), not stories or jokes. Authors' own method; no independent replication. More LLM calls per item.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a two-stage evidence-then-score judge beats plain judging. Cost is more calls.

source: Ha et al. (2024) Organic or Diffused: Can We Distinguish Human Art from AI-generated Images? (CCS 2024)
finding: General users were near chance at telling human art from AI images; professional artists did better; a trained detector was best but fragile.
numbers: 180 crowdworkers, 3,800+ professional artists, 13 expert artists, 5 generators (including Midjourney v6, SDXL, DALL-E 3, Firefly), 7 styles. Professional artists: accuracy 75.32%, FPR 23.53%, FNR 25.37%. Experts 83.44% vs the best detector (Hive) 87.76% on a comparison set. General users described as only slightly better than a coin flip; per-style accuracy for general users 55 to 64% (cartoon 63.58, anime 57.43). Hive on the base set: 98.03% accuracy, 0% FPR. Glaze and added noise cut detector accuracy.
limits: Images from 2023 to 2024 generators. A single overall general-user accuracy was not in the text I read. Survey, not lab.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 (visual art): lay detection is weak; experts are the right rater. Same lesson as text: rater expertise changes the answer.

source: Figueiredo et al. (2025) Echoes of Humanity: Exploring the Perceived Humanness of AI Music
finding: Blind forced-choice test of Suno songs vs human songs: listeners were at chance for random pairs and above chance only when the two songs were similar.
numbers: 308 participants passed checks (of 653 logins); 4 pairs each. Overall success 0.60; random pairs 0.53 (not different from 0.5); similar pairs 0.66 (p<1e-9); similar pairs with lyrics 0.75. Treatment effect of similarity 13 points. In 57% of answers one song was named AI; 20% said both, 16% neither, 7% unsure. Over 10 years of practical music experience raised accuracy (p=0.0009); older age lowered it.
limits: 73% Portuguese speakers. Real-world Suno songs posted by users, not a controlled prompt. Random pairs differ in genre, which can mask AI cues. Human songs from Jamendo.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 (music): modern audio generators are hard for non-experts to detect unless matched. Our own tests should match pairs.

source: Sarmento, Loth, Barthet (2024) Between the AI and Me: listeners' perspectives on AI- and human-composed progressive metal
finding: Listening and reflection study with 32 progressive-metal fans comparing a symbolic AI model (ProgGP) with human tracks, random vs cherry-picked output.
numbers: 32 participants. Factors: generation type, genre (prog metal vs rock control), curation (random vs cherry-picked). Ratings on genre fit, preference, creativity, consistency, playability, humanness, repeatability. Bonferroni threshold p<0.0033.
limits: I read only the abstract and method; per-condition means were not extracted. Small sample of fans.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: curation matters. Cherry-picking is a selection step like our candidate selector; effect size not recorded here.

source: Wikipedia (2025) Experiments in Musical Intelligence, Hofstadter test (re-read for gap 5)
finding: Only one listening test is described: Hofstadter played a real Chopin piece and an EMI Chopin-style piece on a lecture tour and the audience could not do better than chance.
numbers: No audience size, number of trials or accuracy figure is given. No mention of Steve Larson or the Eastman test.
limits: Secondary source; the claim is an unquantified summary.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: no counts or N from a primary text.

source: Ariza (2009) The Interrogator as Critic: The Turing Test and the Evaluation of Generative Music Systems, Computer Music Journal 33(2)
finding: Pointer only. This paper reviews Turing-style evaluation of generative music and is a likely primary source for gap 5; the publisher page returned 403.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened; do not cite for numbers.
agent_relevance: Next step: fetch a repository copy or the Hofstadter (2001) chapter.
